summary: Specifies iTIP, a protocol built on iCalendar objects for scheduling interoperability between calendaring systems. It is independent of any specific transport, so it can be carried over different means of communication, which later documents define.

plainLanguage.summary: iTIP defines how calendar systems use iCalendar objects to exchange invitations, replies, updates, and cancellations. It defines the messages' meaning but leaves the communication method to separate transport specifications.

subtitle: Define calendar scheduling messages independently of how systems transport them.

tldr.problem: Different calendaring systems need shared rules for publishing events, inviting attendees, handling replies, and changing or canceling schedules.
tldr.mechanism: iTIP assigns scheduling meaning to iCalendar objects and methods such as REQUEST, REPLY, CANCEL, and COUNTER, without defining a specific transport.
tldr.outcome: Calendar systems can exchange scheduling transactions over separate transport bindings. RFC 5546 obsoletes RFC 2446 and updates RFC 5545.

today: RFC 5546 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2446 and updates RFC 5545. It is later updated by RFC 6638.

sections.title: A Transport-Independent Scheduling Protocol
sections.content:
The iCalendar Transport-Independent Interoperability Protocol (iTIP) specifies how calendaring systems use iCalendar objects to publish or schedule events, to-dos, journal entries, and busy-time information. It defines application-level messages without requiring a particular way to send them.

A separate transport binding can carry those messages by email, real-time exchange, or another method. The Organizer sends scheduling messages; Attendees respond with status or proposed changes.
sections.plainLanguage: iTIP defines what calendar messages mean, not how they travel between systems. Separate transport specifications can carry the same scheduling messages in different ways.

sections.title: Organizer and Attendee Roles
sections.content:
The Organizer initiates an iTIP exchange, such as proposing a group meeting. Attendees are the Calendar Users included as recipients of the scheduling message; other Calendar Users are not explicitly included.

The Organizer controls the master calendar component. Attendees report their participation status with REPLY and can suggest changes with COUNTER, but they do not directly change the Organizer's component.
sections.plainLanguage: The Organizer owns and updates the shared schedule item. Attendees reply with their status or propose a change for the Organizer to consider.

sections.title: Scheduling Methods
sections.content:
PUBLISH shares an object without expecting an interactive response. REQUEST asks recipients to create or update a calendar item, and REPLY reports an Attendee's status. ADD adds instances to a recurring item; CANCEL removes an item or instance.

REFRESH asks the Organizer for the latest version. COUNTER proposes a change, and DECLINECOUNTER rejects that proposal. Which roles may send each method is defined by iTIP.
sections.plainLanguage: Each method names a different scheduling action, such as inviting, replying, updating, or canceling. The method and calendar data together tell the recipient how to process the message.

sections.title: Matching Updates and Out-of-Order Messages
sections.content:
Calendar systems match components using UID. For an instance of a recurring component, they use UID together with RECURRENCE-ID. SEQUENCE is a secondary key: for the same component, the higher number represents a later revision.

Replies use SEQUENCE to show which revision an Attendee answered. Because messages can arrive out of order, a calendar system compares identifiers and revision numbers instead of assuming messages arrive in sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: UID identifies the calendar item, and RECURRENCE-ID identifies a particular repeat. SEQUENCE helps a system tell newer revisions from older ones when messages arrive out of order.

sections.title: Protecting Scheduling Transactions
sections.content:
iTIP identifies risks including spoofed Organizers or Attendees, unauthorized replacement of an Organizer, eavesdropping, data changes, calendar flooding, and unauthorized refresh requests.

Transport bindings should protect transaction integrity and provide access controls that limit which Calendar Users may schedule with or delegate to others. An Organizer can also send separate messages to keep Attendees from seeing one another's identities.
sections.plainLanguage: Calendar messages can change schedules and reveal who is attending. Transport bindings and access controls should verify senders, protect message contents, and limit who can make scheduling changes.
